title: The Grand New Films About Charles de Gaulle
author: Peter Hitchens
content:
![The Grand New Films About Charles de
Gaulle](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/09/Screenshot-2026-09-24-at-7.19.24
---AM.png)

The future world statesman, in full military uniform, leaps athletically on to
the table. Then he reaches up into the ceiling lamp of his hotel room and
pulls out a concealed microphone. It has been placed there by his American
allies, or perhaps by the perfidious British. Or possibly by both at once.
There are a lot of wires. If there is one brief scene which encapsulates the
two vast new films about Charles de Gaulle, I think this is it. They recount
the astonishing melodrama of the rebirth of France after humiliation and
defeat. And they do so through a patriotic epic about the Second World War in
which Hitler makes no appearance, FDR is the villain, and Churchill often an
American patsy. The hero is the metaphorical and literal (6'5") giant, General
de Gaulle, a man so tall that furniture always seemed too small to him, and so
did most other people.

We owe these films to Julian Jackson's [_peerless
biography_](https://firstthings.com/a-certain-idea-of-
france/?ref=compactmag.com) of de Gaulle, a book that tears through the mind
like a storm. This book (for me at least) revived the forgotten belief that
individual human greatness can force open the grimmest, most unassailable
fortresses. Read it. See the movies. You will not be sorry.
